Each village has its own unique manta pattern,
so when others see you, they recognize what village you come from by the colorful design of your manta.
When I weave outside, I sit on a manta, and whatever I am weaving, whether it is a belt, a hat, or a skirt,
I put a lot of time and effort into each piece.
Market day is special for the women of Chinchero, and we like to dress in our traditional handmade clothes when we go to the market.
We wear colorful jackets, braid our hair, and wear our hats, called monteras, proudly.
In our village everyone wears a montera with a round top.
The brim of the hat curves toward its center, and inside the brim is a secret fold where we can store our money.
When a tourist stops by and purchases one of my textiles, I just pop the money into my hat!
The weaving center helps with the sale of our work, but it is up to each weaver to negotiate a price.
To be honest, I don't make a lot of money, only about three hundred dollars a year.
But I am satisfied when I see how my weaving has made someone happy.
Oh, here is Carla! Someday she will make our village proud and weave beautiful textiles that will tell the story of [i@her@i] generation.

episodes.title: My Life as a Pony Express Rider

subtitle.text: Giddyap! With a good swat to my mustang Bandit's rump, I'm off.
My name is Henry Thompson; I'm 19 years old, and I'm galloping as fast as I can.
Since April of last year, I have ridden for the Central Overland California and Pike's Peak Express Company,
which is the official name for the Pony Express.
My route in Nevada, from Fort Churchill to Friday's Station,
is only one part of a large network of routes that have made it possible to send news, letters,
and other important papers all the way across the country.
I'm proud to be a part of the Pony Express, which takes the mail from St. Joseph, Missouri, to San Francisco, California, in about ten days.
But today, November 17, 1861, is my last ride, because the telegraph line joining both coasts of America went into operation about three weeks ago.
Soon there will be no more need for the Pony Express.
Eighteen months ago I was picked from the many young men who answered a newspaper advertisement in Sacramento, California.
The company wanted skilled riders weighing less than 120 pounds, which describes me perfectly, since I'm skinny as a rail and an excellent rider.
The weight the horses carry must be as low as possible because they run very hard.
The horses we ride aren't really ponies, but they're small, which is probably why the company got the nickname "Pony Express."
To make it easier on our horses, I'm only allowed to carry 25 pounds of equipment, like some food and my Colt revolver.
Of course I also carry an additional twenty pounds of mail in a mochila, a leather saddlebag.
I was assigned to the Fort Churchill home station, and I've learned my route well.
It's one of the hardest routes, because I have to go high into the Sierra Nevada Mountains.
You'd think the Pony Express carries the mail only by horse, but that's not exactly true.
The mail usually travels between San Francisco and Sacramento by boat.
Between the east and St. Joseph, Missouri, the mail travels by stagecoach.
But riders on horseback are needed between St. Joseph and Sacramento because it's rough country—
through the deserts of the Great Basin and over the mountains.
There are home stations, where the riders live between trips, every 75 to 100 miles,
and relay stations, where the riders can change horses, every 10 to 15 miles.
Saddling up a fresh horse usually takes less than two minutes, and then we're off again to the next relay station.
My route is about 75 miles, but other routes are longer.
Special, lightweight saddles make the horses' jobs easier.
I sling the mochila over the saddle and secure it over the saddle's horn.
Most of the time we carry about fifty pieces of mail, which are placed in four leather boxes sewn into the corners of the mochila.
When the Pony Express started, the price to deliver a piece of mail was five dollars for each half ounce.
Only the wealthiest people use our service; although we've dropped the price to one dollar now, that's still a lot of money.
Our service is expensive because it's the quickest.
Before the Pony Express, mail from New York to San Francisco took about four weeks—and often longer—
because it had to be shipped down the East Coast to the Isthmus of Panama, transported by rail overland,
and then shipped up the West Coast by steamship.
But President Abraham Lincoln's inaugural address made it to California in 7 days and 17 hours—
because it was telegraphed to Nebraska and then traveled on the Pony Express.
The rider from the east arrived at Fort Churchill at six o'clock tonight, and I left right away.
I'm so grateful the moon is full.
Although I know this route like the back of my hand, I don't want anything bad to happen on my last ride.
As I head toward Reed's Station, I remember the day I rode through a forest of aspens, where Indians were hiding.
I crouched over my horse's neck and rode as fast as I could, shooting behind me the whole time—
that was the fastest I have ever ridden in my whole life.
As I get close to Reed's Station, I blow a horn four times to alert the stationmaster that I'm coming in.
A fresh horse is ready for me, and I immediately set off for Dayton.
That little town sprang up just recently because gold was discovered nearby.
Riding through a hemlock forest, I have to be careful my horse doesn't stumble in the dark, because a few riders have been hurt this way.
But once we're out of the woods, there are places where I can let him run as fast as he wants on this chilly, moonlit night.
Pony Express horses are specially selected for their speed and endurance,
and they can gallop up to 25 miles per hour; usually, though, we ride at about 10 miles per hour to save the horses' energy.
After a brief stop at Carson City, it's a fairly easy 15-mile ride to Genoa, but the hardest part of my trip is still ahead of me.
With a fresh horse, I head into the Sierra Nevada Mountains.
This stretch of the ride is only about ten miles, but the uphill climb is extremely difficult.
Halfway up I find myself in six inches of snow, and I must slow down— slipping on the rocky slopes would be a costly delay.
Soon, though, I see the light reflecting off Lake Tahoe, and both my horse and I are relieved to finally arrive at our destination, Friday's Station,
and pass the mochila on to the next rider.
Now I'm going to take off my boots, grab a bowl of beans, and sit by the fire as I think of all the men that made the Pony Express possible.
Some are no longer with us, killed by Indians or robbers or the weather.
After I rest a bit, I'll probably head east, where I hear the Union Army is looking for some good riders.
After being a Pony Express rider, I'm used to danger.
It's time for me to look for a new adventure.

episodes.title: My Life as a Portuguese Explorer

subtitle.text: My ship sails in the morning from the port of Lagos, Portugal.
I'm supervising my sailors as they lower crates into the cargo area, check the sails for tears and holes, and test the ropes.
India is our destination, by order of Prince Henry of Portugal, and we will be exploring seas we've never seen before.
My name is Edmundo Veloso. The year is 1434, and I have just been promoted to captain of the [i@Terra Nova,@i] a ship both fast and true.
I am full of curiosity and armed with tools that have served mariners for years and years and the latest charts.
This is the opportunity I've been working for.
I first set foot on a ship at age 12 when, without warning, my father took me to the docks and set me up as an apprentice on a ship.
I came from a big family, and my father could not afford to feed everyone.
So over the next twenty years, I learned everything about sailing.
I swabbed the decks and polished the brass.
I learned how to rig the sails, navigate, and steer the ship.
Climbing the rigging like a monkey to set the sails was more than a job for me; it was the most fun I ever had.
The crow's nest, high atop the highest mast, was my favorite place.
Although I was not enchanted with the sea as a child, I became enchanted as I grew up on it.
The reign of Prince Henry of Portugal is an exciting time to be a mariner.
Henry's goal is to find a sea route to India by heading south along the west coast of Africa.
A man of science, Prince Henry wants to find a faster route to trade for spices and precious metals from the East,
to spread Christianity, and perhaps even to discover new fishing grounds.
The port of Lagos is close to Prince Henry's villa,
where I had dinner a few nights ago and met cartographers, astrologers, navigators, and other explorers.
It was an inspiring evening, and I came to understand Henry's plan—
to use scientific methods in exploration and publish our findings for the benefit of those who come after us.
Among the tools I use to navigate are the nocturnal, the astrolabe, and the mariner's compass.
The nocturnal allows me to determine the time at night.
I locate the Big Dipper, stars in an easy-to-see constellation.
Two of its stars line up and point to the North Star— that's why they're called pointer stars.
I line up the hole in the center of my nocturnal with the North Star.
Then I swing the long arm of the nocturnal until it lines up with the Big Dipper's pointer stars and read the time!
With the astrolabe I find my position by measuring how high the noon sun is over the horizon.
From that measurement I can determine latitude—how far north or south our ship is from the equator.
My mariner's compass has a magnetized needle that points north, which also helps me determine my position—along with my sea charts of course.
These charts have lines that have been drawn to show the direction of the winds, as well as descriptions of landmarks,
which I also use to figure out where I am.
I keep a record of the time I sail on each bearing (direction) on the compass.
With this method, my tools, and my years of experience, I navigate with certainty on the open seas.
Seven years ago I was the first mate on the ship that discovered the Azores Islands.
Having no land in sight was worrisome since we couldn't rely on our sea charts, but the results were well worth it—discovering a new land!
Tomorrow we will sail south along the African coast.
My ship, a caravel, carries different types of sails, which will allow us to maneuver easily and quickly in the wind.
Long, thin, and shallow, the caravel is exceptional for exploring the coasts.
It has taken time to assemble my crew of twenty, but they are ready.
Many of them are young men who remind me of myself at that age—full of excitement.
These young sailors are apprehensive, but their curiosity and sense of adventure overcome their fear.
The older men are experienced, and because of this, they know the sea is unforgiving.
They realize the weather can change in a moment.
One morning the sky can be blue and the sea calm.
But by noon a storm might arise, creating giant waves that can capsize any ship.
All my men are superstitious and fearful at times.
For instance, some believe the farther south one sails, the hotter the water becomes, because the sea gets colder as one sails northward.
They fear southern seas will boil them.
Others believe we will reach the edge of the earth and fall off, or that monsters lurk in the deep, just waiting for an unsuspecting ship.
Many who have families are not willing to take the risk of a long sea voyage.
I respect their fears because, in fact, I am not immune to them now that I have a family of my own.
But to me this trip is the climax of my career.
I tell the crew of my pride in being on the first ship to sight the Azores and how this trip will be just as memorable,
but in the end, I release anyone who is hesitant.
In uncharted waters I will need commitment not fear.
I will need collaboration not dissent. I will need boldness to face whatever we may have to face.
And so my crew is mostly young, with a few adventurous old sailors who will help me guide us to safe harbors.
We are poised at the beginning of a voyage of discovery. What will the outcome be?
Will we come back triumphant with charts of new shores to add to Prince Henry's fame, or will we never be heard from again?
Good day! My name is Melanie Hoff, and I'm a thirty-year-old zookeeper at the Auckland Zoo in New Zealand.
I've been a zookeeper for seven years,
but even now, in 2009, each day feels like a new beginning because you never know what to expect when animals are involved.
Right now I am working with tigers and cheetahs.
Last year something very extraordinary happened with our Sumatran tigers, Molek and Oz—they became the proud parents of three tiger cubs.
But before I get into that, let me tell you a bit more about how I became a zookeeper.
As a little girl, I loved animals. I had a pet hamster and two dogs.
My father was a veterinarian—an animal doctor—and every summer he would volunteer at the zoo.
Sometimes I accompanied him, and I would spend my time following all the zookeepers around, asking lots of questions.
I found out quickly that zoos aren't just parks where wild and exotic animals are on display.
Zoos are places that create public awareness about the kinds of animals in our world, how they live, and how to protect them.
In college I studied zoology, a branch of biology that deals with animals and animal life.
I learned how to classify animals—from starfish to elephants—
and by the time I graduated, I knew all about how different animals behave, what they like to eat, and where they live.
Classroom study is very important, but zoos need people with hands-on experience with animals too.
So I volunteered at the zoo, just like my dad.
Right now I am taking care of our Sumatran tigers, which are the smallest of all tiger species.
They are found in the wild only on the Indonesian island of Sumatra—nowhere else.
Sumatran tigers are threatened because of the loss of their natural habitat and illegal poaching.
Their habitat is being destroyed in part because the trees are being logged to make paper.
And they are killed because tiger bones are used in traditional Chinese medicine, and hunters want their teeth and claws for trophies.
It is part of my job to educate people about endangered species, but my first priority is to take care of the tigers to the best of my ability.
My day starts around 7:30 a.m. Every morning the zookeepers from the different animal areas in the zoo have a brief meeting.
We discuss any changes in the behavior, diet, skin quality, or coat condition of the animals in our care.
Next my coworkers and I prepare food for the tigers, which is usually meat on the bone.
We hide the food throughout the exhibit so our tigers can experience more natural foraging behavior.
Then, from 8:15 until noon, we clean the animal enclosures and the exhibit areas.
During cleaning the tigers are moved back and forth between the different areas or kept in cages in the tiger house.
Most enclosures usually have ponds and climbing surfaces within a natural-looking environment.
The water needs to be fresh, and all the areas where the animals spend time are secure and safe for both the animals and zoo personnel.
New animals arrive at our zoo all the time; some are from other zoos, while others are rescued from the wild.
If they are sharing an enclosure, they need to learn to get along with the other animals, so training is very important.
For example, a zookeeper communicates with clear signals,
which can be gestures or vocal cues, to tell animals to enter or exit certain sections of their enclosures.
At our zoo we have two very friendly Asian elephants.
Their keeper has trained these gigantic creatures to walk around the zoo and remain calm even when excited visitors scream with delight.
We also have daily animal encounters:
specified times when visitors can see and learn about some of their favorite animals—such as giraffes, orangutans, and even snakes—up close.
The keepers explain the animals' habits, what they like to eat, and how they like to play.
Sometimes the zookeepers will allow visitors to pet some of the animals, but safety is always a top priority.
It's important to remember that the zoo is not a circus.
In the past zoo animals were kept in small cages and made to do tricks to entertain people. Thankfully things have changed.
As you can see, being a zookeeper is a lot of work, but it's also a lot of fun.
One time a television crew was filming at our zoo, and the soundman held up a big microphone with a fluffy cover on it.
One of our cheetahs noticed this fluffy thing and decided to play with it.
People burst out laughing. But scary things happen too.
One day I surprised a gorilla when I touched her, and she turned around and almost bit my hand.
It was entirely my fault, and I was reminded again that these are wild animals.
The saddest part of my job is when an animal dies.
I still remember when Nisha, one of our Sumatran tigers, died in May 2006.
All of us at the zoo still miss her.
But the best part of my job is when we welcome new animal babies into our zoo family.
In early 2008 Nisha's younger sister Molek mated with Oz, another Sumatran tiger, and gave birth in June to three cubs―two males and one female.
The entire country was ecstatic over the news!
Being a zookeeper doesn't pay very well, and it involves long hours.
So why do so many people want to become zookeepers?
Because we love animals and want to draw attention to the fragile planet we all live on together.
For example, fewer than four hundred Sumatran tigers remain in the wild,
so the publicity surrounding the birth of these cubs educated people about how endangered Sumatran tigers are.
Suddenly everyone wanted to help save Sumatran tigers from extinction.
Through education the public comes to understand the need to preserve any species that is in danger of being destroyed and lost forever.
I believe there is nothing more rewarding than my work as a zookeeper.
It is the best job a human can do for the earth and all its living things.
My name is Othon le Quarrelier, and I come from a family of stonemasons living in the town of Rouen, France.
Of course I am a stonemason too.
I wouldn't do anything else because over the centuries stonemasons have built marvelous structures in every corner of the world,
from the Egyptian pyramids to the Parthenon in Greece.
We stonemasons have always been in demand for our great skills, and the work we do, cutting and shaping stone, hasn't changed much.
But at this time, in 1220, stonemasons are building a greater variety of structures—bridges, cathedrals, and castles—than ever before.
My father was a master stonemason, but he did not teach me the trade.
He paid another master mason nearby to take me on as an apprentice when I was 11 years old.
I lived with this master mason for seven years to learn the craft.
I was taught how to select stone from the quarry, a deep excavation pit outside of town that contains the material we use.
Then I learned how to use the tools of masonry: hammers, chisels, the compass, and the set square.
The set square helps me make sure the walls I build are straight and true, so that my corners form ninety-degree angles.
I learned how to use my hammer and chisel to turn a rough block of stone into a carved and polished building block.
My master showed me how to work the stone carefully and patiently, and how to place the finished stone into position in a wall and set it in mortar.
Eventually I left my teacher and began the life of a journeyman, someone who has finished his apprenticeship but is not yet a master mason.
Journeyman masons often travel from place to place, looking for work.
Whenever I came to a new town, I'd visit the local guildhall, a place where a stonemason can find a job, a place to sleep, and good food.
Master masons at the guildhall test the journeymen, and if they're skilled and pass the test, the master masons hire them.
Once a journeyman gets a job, he chisels his personal mark on the stone he carves so the master mason can evaluate his work.
Some of the buildings that stonemasons create are so tall and beautiful that many people believe our skills must be magical.
But the secret to our success is geometry, which we learn early in our apprenticeship.
Geometry is a branch of mathematics that involves the relationships between lines and angles,
and the size, shape, and position of objects within space. Geometry makes masonry possible.
After working as a journeyman for a number of years, I acquired the skills to become a master mason,
and now I direct the masonry work at the cathedral in Chartres.
Twenty-six years ago, in 1194, most of the building was destroyed when a lightning strike caused a huge fire,
which consumed a lot of the town as well.
People were very upset since the town was a popular pilgrimage destination.
So the local bishop decided to rebuild the cathedral and make it much grander.
It's taken a long time, but we're almost finished.
Since I am responsible for the entire project, I hire the journeymen masons, carpenters, glassmakers, and all the other laborers necessary.
Over two hundred people work for me, and I live in a temporary house right next to the construction site so I'm always on hand to supervise the work.
My stonemasons are divided into two groups: one group works at the quarry five miles away, cutting and shaping the rocks,
and the other group polishes the stone blocks on-site and sets them in place with mortar.
To cut the rocks, a mason uses a number of tools, including axes, chisels, and hammers.
The ax is used to hack at the rock to remove large chunks of unwanted stone.
To make the rock even smaller, a mason uses a chisel to chip off smaller pieces of rock.
By doing this at the quarry, we greatly reduce the rock's weight, which makes it easier to transport to the building site.
The previous cathedral was small and had very few windows, so it was dark and gloomy inside.
The new church has tall towers that seem to climb up to heaven and huge stained-glass windows that fill the cathedral with light.
To achieve these breathtaking effects, I used full-scale drawings on plaster on the site's floor.
They helped me visualize the project and calculate the amounts of materials and the number of men I would need.
For this cathedral we worked from the early spring through the warm months, which allowed the mortar holding the stones in place to dry thoroughly.
During the winter construction stopped, and the masons carved the statues on the west wall of the cathedral.
Notice how their robes make the vertical lines of the soaring structure seem even taller.
The masons also carved other smaller statues—such as gargoyles,
which direct rainwater away from the building so it does not damage the foundation.
Masons must pay very close attention to small details.
As the cathedral began to rise, my masons had to work at great heights—very dangerous work.
My former teacher was badly hurt when he fell during the construction of the cathedral in Reims.
Getting building materials to these heights was difficult, but we managed.
We accomplished this by leaving openings, called putlog holes, in the stone at regular intervals.
We used the holes to hold logs on which we placed wood planks to create platforms that can be reached by a ladder.
Then we used special cranes to hoist the stone up to our workmen on the platforms.
When the building is finished, the logs and platforms will be removed and the putlog holes filled in with mortar.
It can be dangerous work, but I love working with stone.
And I'm proud that this cathedral will live on after me.
It will proclaim to future generations that whenever the highest quality of craftsmanship is needed, stonemasons will be there.
The desert wilderness has many names in the Bedu language, my native tongue, because the desert has many faces.
Some parts of the desert have dunes as high as two hundred meters, and other parts are flat and sandy.
Dry riverbeds can suddenly become raging rivers when the rain falls hard and fast.
After those rare rainstorms, our desert blossoms for a short while into wide carpets of grass and beautiful wildflowers.
My people are always on the move through the deserts of Arabia, tending our camels and goats.
We never stay in one place very long, but we enjoy the region around the oasis at Al-Hasa the most.
The year is 1670, and my name is Karim Abu Sukar.
I am a member of the Bani Khalid tribe. It is a great honor to meet you.
My people are called Bedouin, and we spend our lives wandering throughout the desert.
But believe me, my friend, we always know exactly where we are going and why.
When my family travels from water hole to water hole, all our animals travel with us.
My sweet wife, Rana, is the wonderful mother of our son, Falid, who is with our herd of goats right now.
She takes care of our tent, which is made of goat hair and easily portable.
You can see that the tent is divided into two sections: one for the men and one for the women.
All the cooking utensils are stored on Rana's side of the tent, and we entertain our guests on my side.
Look at the beautiful curtain Rana has made to divide our tent!
In fact, Rana wove the tent, the carpets we are sitting on, and even my clothes.
Falid and I couldn't live without her and her many talents.
When our family and friends gather to eat and drink coffee, we like to tell stories.
Some tales are about our brave ancestors and their many adventures— about living and fighting in the desert.
Other stories are about a wise fool named Goha.
These stories are always the funniest. Would you like to hear one?
I think "Goha's Kettle" would be fitting for this occasion.
One day Goha borrowed a large pot from a neighbor.
Several days later he returned it, but with a smaller pot inside.
His neighbor stared at the little pot in surprise and asked Goha, "Where did this come from?"
"The big pot gave birth," Goha replied matter-of-factly.
Laughing at Goha's foolishness and happy at his own good fortune, the neighbor took both pots.
A few weeks later, Goha asked his neighbor whether he could borrow the large pot again.
The neighbor eagerly lent it to him of course.
But months went by, and Goha did not return the pot.
The neighbor became more and more upset.
At last he went to Goha and asked for it.
"My good friend, something horrible has happened.
Your pot died," replied Goha. Shocked, his neighbor screamed, "Died? Since when do kettles die?"
"Ever since they've been able to have children," Goha answered. That is a good story!
Come, it is getting late, and I must go to my son, who is tending our goats not far from here.
My father showed me all the best spots for grazing goats, and he knew of these places because his father had taught him,
so my herd is one of the largest.
I have taught Falid to care for the herd as well.
Our black goats survive well in the desert.
They eat almost anything that grows, which is good because very little grows in the desert except for woody shrubs and an occasional weed.
Black goats are special because they can survive without water for four days, so we can graze our herd far from the water holes.
Our goats produce milk for our family, and we use everything from the animal—hair, skin, and dung. Nothing goes to waste!
The goat hair is used to make our tents and blankets,
the hides are used to make bags to carry our water, and the dung is used as fuel for our fires.
When we host a feast, we love to roast a whole goat using our traditional underground oven.
We dig a deep hole and line the inside with clay and stones.
Then we burn wood in the bottom of the hole until it turns to charcoal.
Finally we skewer a skinned goat and suspend it above the charcoal on a spit.
We add some spices and roast the goat for many hours, turning it once in a while.
The aroma is wonderful, and the smoke makes our mouths water as it winds around our camp.
My tribe has existed in this region for a very long time and fought many battles with other tribes.
The grazing lands that we use and the water holes where we drink belong to our tribe—the ancient and noble Bani Khalid tribe.
Each tent represents a family, and our tent is part of a larger group of tents called a camp.
All the people who live in our camp are closely related, and everyone in the camp is related to an even larger group called a clan.
A number of related clans make up an even larger group called a tribe.
Each family, camp, and clan is headed by an elder, and the entire tribe has a leader.
But never forget that the Bedouin are independent people—we like complete freedom.
We live in a harsh land, so we live simply.
Our people are always courteous and generous to one another and to our guests because we consider it our duty, and honor is very important to us.
There is my son. We had better get back to our tent.
Rana is waiting for us with something special to eat.
Come, I know many more Goha stories to make you laugh!
